readerTitle: Every team hit its target. The customer still left angry.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방 리모델링 회사, 레스토랑) + 실제 연구 (Kerr 1975, 보상 설계의 고전 논문)
insight: 서로 일을 넘겨받는 팀들을 각자의 숫자로만 보상하면, 각 팀은 자기 비용을 다음 팀에게 떠넘기는 법을 배운다. 보상의 일부는 팀이 함께 만드는 결과에 묶어야 한다.
misconception: 팀마다 목표를 분명히 주고 그 목표를 잘 달성하게 하면, 모든 팀의 성과를 더한 것이 회사의 성과가 된다.

sources.text: Kerr, S. (1975). On the Folly of Rewarding A, While Hoping for B. Academy of Management Journal, 18(4).
리모델링 회사와 레스토랑 사례는 설명용 가상 예시이며 수치를 쓰지 않음

factChecks.note: Kerr(1975) 논문의 학술지명·권호(Academy of Management Journal 18권 4호)를 게시 전 확인하세요. 1995년 Academy of Management Executive에 재게재된 판본도 있습니다. 카드에는 연도와 제목의 요지만 적었습니다.
공동 성과 보상에서 팀이 커질수록 무임승차와 '가시성(line of sight)' 저하가 생긴다는 점은 보상 설계 분야의 일반적 논의로 서술했습니다. 특정 수치나 연구 결과는 인용하지 않았습니다.
리모델링 회사·레스토랑·구매팀 사례는 모두 가상이며 수치가 없습니다. 실제 기업 사실로 오해되지 않도록 illustrative 표시를 확인하세요.

cards.title: Every team hit its target. The customer still left angry.
body: A kitchen remodeling company has its best quarter ever. Sales signed record contracts. The install crews finished jobs faster than planned.
Both teams earned full bonuses. Meanwhile, complaints and refund requests climbed, and profit per job fell. Nobody broke a rule.

image.label: Two teams celebrating while a customer frowns in an unfinished kitchen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 트로피를 든 영업팀, 오른쪽에 트로피를 든 시공팀. 가운데에는 문짝이 비뚤어지고 마감이 덜 된 주방 앞에서 팔짱 낀 고객. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your remodeling teams are both winning.
body: Salespeople earn commission on contract value. Installers get a bonus for finishing within the estimated hours.
Sales keep promising custom extras and tight dates. Crews rush the finishing work to stay on hours. What do you change first?

options.text: Retrain the sales team to stop overpromising
options.feedback: It may help for a month. But the commission still pays for bigger promises, so the pressure comes back.

options.text: Pay both teams partly on the same result: job profit and the customer's rating at handover
options.feedback: Now each team gains when the other succeeds. You give up some simplicity, and each person controls only part of the result.

options.text: Hire a quality inspector to check every finished job
options.feedback: You catch more bad work, at a new cost. But both teams are still paid to create the problems the inspector finds.

cards.title: Each team did exactly what it was paid to do.
body: Sales won by making contracts bigger. Extras and fast dates closed deals, and the cost of delivering them landed on the crews.
Crews won by saving hours. Skipped touch-ups and rushed fittings saved time, and the cost landed on the customer and the warranty budget.
No single team owned the whole job. So the whole job got worse while every scorecard looked great.

cards.title: Incentives across teams
body: When teams depend on each other, **rewarding each one only on its own number** teaches it to push costs onto the next team. Each part looks better. The whole gets worse.

Management researcher Steven Kerr named this pattern in a 1975 paper, *On the Folly of Rewarding A, While Hoping for B*. Companies hope for one result and pay for another, then are surprised by what they get.

image.label: Relay of teams passing a box that grows heavier at each handoff
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 영업 → 시공 → 고객 순서로 상자를 건네는 릴레이. 각 팀 머리 위에는 초록 체크(목표 달성), 상자는 건널 때마다 커지고 무거워져 마지막 고객이 힘겹게 받음.

cards.title: Follow the cost to where it lands.
body: Good cross-team incentives start at the handoffs, not the teams.
list: **Map the handoffs:** where does one team's output become another team's input?
**Ask where the cost goes:** if this team wins, who pays for it?
**Share part of the reward:** tie a slice of each team's pay to the result they create together
**Add a counterweight:** pair speed with quality, or volume with profit
cards.callout: Teams stop dumping costs on each other when they share the bill.

cards.title: The same trap hides inside every company.
body: A factory's purchasing team is rewarded for the lowest price per part. It switches to a cheaper supplier. The production line then spends weeks dealing with more defects. Purchasing's number improved. The plant's did not.
The fix is the same: judge purchasing partly on the cost of parts *after* defects and delays, not just on the invoice.
cards.softwareNote: Sales paid on new bookings may offer deep discounts to customers who are a poor fit. The churn lands on customer success months later. Many software firms pay part of commission only if the customer is still active after a set period.

cards.title: Shared goals can blur who owns what.
body: If everyone is paid only on company profit, no one sees how their own work moves the number. Some people coast while others carry the load.
Keep a mix: each team still owns a measure it fully controls, plus a shared measure it can clearly influence. Shared groups work best when they are small enough that people see each other's effort.
And pay isn't the only lever. Joint reviews and shared customer feedback also change behavior.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: The head chef's bonus depends on keeping food costs low. Servers earn a bonus on average check size.
The kitchen shrinks portions and drops a costly dish guests love. Servers push add-ons that swamp the kitchen at peak hours. Wait times and reviews get worse. What do you do?

options.text: Replace both bonuses with one bonus on monthly restaurant profit
options.feedback: Now everyone shares the result. But the chef and a server can barely see how their own shift moves monthly profit, so the bonus may motivate little.

options.text: Keep each team's measure, and add a shared one both affect: ticket times and guest ratings
options.feedback: Each team keeps a number it controls, and both now gain from a smooth, well-reviewed service. It takes more tracking and a fair way to share the bonus.

options.text: Loosen the chef's food cost target so portions grow back
options.feedback: Portions may return, but servers are still paid to overload the kitchen. You fixed one symptom and kept the conflict.

cards.title: Pay teams for the handoff, not just their half.
body: When one team's win becomes another team's cost, separate targets will pull them apart. Tie part of the reward to what they deliver together.
**Try it today:** pick two teams that hand work to each other. Write down what each is rewarded for. Then ask: if one team hits its target, what does it cost the other?
